info.title: FixMate API
info.summary: The JSON API the four FixMate applications talk to.
info.description:
A JSON API and nothing else: no route in it returns a page.

There are four sign-in doors, one per account type, and each resolves credentials against its own store. A person may hold an account in several stores under one address, so which store a request reaches is decided by the URL and never by the address in the body.

Every route below `/api/v1/identity` and above it is described by three artifacts that must agree: this document, `contract.json` (the front ends' recorded expectation), and the back end's route table. `php artisan api-docs:check` and `php artisan api-client:check` each hold one link of that chain.

servers.description: The application's own origin. Every path in this document is absolute, including the /api prefix, so that it can be compared to the back end's route table without arithmetic on a base path.

tags.name: Customer

tags.description: The worker application, and the `workers` credential store.

tags.name: Super administrator

tags.description: The public product catalogue. The one surface on this API that carries no credential: it is readable by anyone, which is a property of the route and not an oversight.

post.summary: Sign in as an end user.
post.description:
Resolves the credentials against the `users` store only, so it can only ever succeed for an account that exists there.

An unknown address, a wrong password and an account that cannot be used all answer with the same 422 and the same message, because telling them apart would make this endpoint a way of asking which addresses hold accounts.

200.description: The token, and the account it belongs to.

post.description: A separate door from the customer one, backed by a separate store. The worker is returned under `worker`, not under `user`, so a worker application is never handed a key it would have to special-case.

200.description: The token, and the account it belongs to.

post.description: A separate door from the super administrator one, backed by a separate store. An account that can sign in here carries no account-management ability; that is the distinction between the two administrator doors, and it is enforced here rather than in the interface.

200.description: The token, and the account it belongs to.

post.summary: Sign in as a super administrator.
post.description: The only path in the platform that issues the wildcard ability. The account is returned under `super_admin`.

200.description: The token, and the account it belongs to.

post.summary: Ask for a customer password reset link.
post.description:
Answers the same way whether or not the address holds an account, because a reset endpoint that reported an unknown address would be a way of asking which addresses do. A screen rendering the acknowledgement is showing a conditional statement and must not present it as "we have emailed you".

The store the address is looked for in is not a field, and must never become one: it is decided by the endpoint this request arrived at, so a client cannot ask for a link against a store that is not its own.

The link is single use and it is checked before the password is, so a password refused under `errors.password` leaves the link usable. A link that is spent or has expired is refused under `errors.password_reset` — a different failure with a different fix, told apart here even though neither says whether an account exists.

Not throttled, unlike the link request: this endpoint cannot be flooded with mail.

post.summary: Ask for a worker password reset link.
post.description: The same neutral acknowledgement as the customer door, against the `workers` store. Throttled separately from sign-in, and separately from the other three stores' reset doors, so flooding one store does not lock the same address out of another.

A separate operation from the customer one rather than a shared one with a parameter: the store a reset changes is decided by the endpoint, and a front end that could name the store would be able to ask for a link against an account that is not its own.

post.summary: Ask for an administrator password reset link.
post.description: Against the `admins` store, whichever store the address also happens to hold accounts in.
The same two refusal fields as every other reset, against the `admins` store.

post.summary: Ask for a super administrator password reset link.
post.description: Against the `super_admins` store.

post.summary: Redeem a super administrator reset link.
post.description: The same two refusal fields as every other reset, against the `super_admins` store.

get.summary: Ask who the customer application's token belongs to.
get.description:
One door per application rather than one shared route, so that "a worker's token does not open the customer application" is a fact about a real address. A token presented at the wrong door is refused with a 403 that names both account types, which is safe to say because the caller has already proved they hold a working token.

`account_type` is in the response so a front end can notice it holds the wrong token. Without it, a mismatched token renders an empty dashboard rather than an error.

Worth calling at start-up rather than trusting a token handed over from storage: a suspended account is refused here with a 403, because an access token outlives the decision that issued it.

200.description: The account the token belongs to, and the abilities on the token.

get.summary: Ask who the worker application's token belongs to.
get.description: The same response as every other door, refused for the same reasons. The account type comes back as `workers`.

200.description: The account the token belongs to, and the abilities on the token.

get.summary: Ask who the administrator application's token belongs to.
get.description: The same response as every other door, refused for the same reasons. The account type comes back as `admins`.

200.description: The account the token belongs to, and the abilities on the token.

get.summary: Ask who the super administrator application's token belongs to.
get.description: The same response as every other door, refused for the same reasons. The account type comes back as `super_admins`.

200.description: The account the token belongs to, and the abilities on the token.

get.description:
A super administrator function. The token must belong to a super administrator and carry `accounts:read`; an administrator is refused with a 403 whether or not the identifier in the path exists.

That is deliberate. A 404 for a record you may not see would make this endpoint a way of discovering which administrator accounts exist, so a caller that receives a 404 can be sure it was allowed to ask. The identifier is a positive integer, so anything else is a 404 rather than a server error.

The identifier is not a bound model, and must not become one: model binding resolves before the authorisation middleware runs, so a bound model would answer 404 for an identifier that does not exist and 403 for one that does — the same oracle, reintroduced.

200.description: The administrator's record.

post.description:
Exchange a renewal token for a new access token and a new renewal token. The renewal token travels in the `Authorization` header, so there is no request body and no field in which a token could be logged.

The presented token is spent by this call. That is the design: a renewal token is held in browser storage, where injected script can read it, so it is worth one use and a short life. Presenting it twice is not "slightly behind" — the second attempt is a 401 and the session is over.

A renewal token may call this route and nothing else. `account.can` refuses it everywhere else, and this route refuses an access token in return, so neither credential can be used as the other.

**This route answers even when the account must change its password.** `EnsurePasswordChanged` exempts it, sign-out and the change itself. The exemption is safe because the access token returned here is still refused by that guard on every other route: a renewal mints a token that can reach nothing, so it cannot be used to walk around the rule, and refusing it only meant that a person who refreshed the change-password screen was signed out and told their account could not be used. `must_change_password` in the response is what lets a front end put them back where they were.

200.description: A new access token, and the renewal token that replaces the one just spent.

post.summary: Sign out of every customer session.
post.description:
Revoke every token this account holds, in all four applications.

All of them, not the one presented, because a person who signs out of one application while signed in to another expects to be signed out of both — and a front end cannot reach into another application's memory to do it, so the guarantee has to be that the credential the other application holds stops being accepted.

The renewal tokens go too, which is what stops the sign-out being undone by a page load.

This route is guarded by the token alone, with no `account.can`. Refusing a renewal token here would break the commonest case: an expired access token is the normal reason to sign out, and the renewal token is the credential still alive. Revoking tokens can only affect the account presenting them.

200.description: Every token this account held has been revoked.

post.x-authorisation: The token alone. Deliberately not `account.can`, which would refuse a renewal token — and an expired access token is the normal reason for signing out, so refusing the renewal token would leave a working one in storage that signs the person straight back in. Revoking tokens can only affect the account presenting them, so there is nothing for an account-type guard to protect.

get.summary: Every account in the platform, across all four account types.
get.description:
One flat list rather than four named sections, because the question this answers is "who has access anywhere in this system" and four screens cannot answer it. Rows are grouped by account type, then by identifier within each type, so the order is total and a person comparing two moments sees rows in the same places.

Suspended and pending accounts are included. A directory that hid them would make a suspension indistinguishable from a deletion, which is the outcome this whole surface exists to avoid.

The caller appears in their own listing. That is not a leak: a super administrator auditing who has access can see themselves.

200.description: Every account, of every type.

post.summary: Suspend one administrator, keeping the record.
post.description:
Takes no request body. The only question is whether, and the path already answers it; a body would be somewhere for a caller to put a status of their own choosing, and the back end would ignore it.

The status is set to `suspended` and nothing else changes: the name, the address and the password hash are copied through, so restoring the account is a status change back rather than an invitation. There is no delete route on this surface at all — an account that can be removed is an account whose history can be removed with it.

**No tokens are revoked, and none need to be.** Both authorisation middlewares re-read the account's status on every request, so changing it closes the access door and the renewal door on the very next request, with no window in which a suspended person keeps working by never reloading. Revoking here as well would be a second copy of that guarantee in a place that does not run on the read path.

parameters.name: admin
parameters.description: The administrator's identifier. A positive integer, so anything else is a 404 rather than a server error.

200.description: The administrator's record, now suspended.

post.summary: Promote one administrator to super administrator.
post.description:
Takes no request body. The only question is whether, and the path already answers it; a body would be somewhere for a caller to put a status of their own choosing, and the back end would ignore it.

A record is **created**, not a flag set. Super administrators live in their own table, so promotion inserts a `super_admins` row carrying the same identity and the same password hash — which is what keeps the most powerful account type a small countable set instead of a boolean on a table anybody with `accounts:read` can read.

The administrator record is then **suspended, not deleted**. Access moved between the two tables, and the record of what that person did while they were an administrator has to outlive their promotion.

`warning` is null while the role is narrow and carries a sentence once it is not. The threshold belongs to the back end and so does the wording; a front end that re-derived the count from the sentence would be a second threshold in a second language.

parameters.name: admin
parameters.description: The administrator's identifier. A positive integer, so anything else is a 404 rather than a server error.

200.description: The new super administrator account, and a warning if the role has become too wide.

post.description:
Replaces the password of whoever is signed in and withdraws every other session that account held.

**`current_password` is required and is not a convenience.** The access token proves who is asking; the current password proves it is the person rather than a copy of their session. Without it, anybody who found a token could set a new password and lock the real owner out permanently.

**The account comes from the token.** There is no identifier in the path and none in the body, so there is nothing for a caller to change in order to reach an account that is not theirs. The only selector is the account type in the path, and the guard checks it - an end user's token is refused at the administrators' door.

**Every other session is withdrawn**, on every device, because a session opened with the old password keeps working however new the stored hash is. The session making the change is spared, so the person is not signed out of the application they are standing in.

The new password is checked against the same policy the reset flow uses, and may not be the current one - otherwise "you must change your password" could be satisfied by submitting the shared password again, and the flag cleared with nothing changed.

One door per account type, matching the `me`, renew and sign-out routes. The account type is a literal in both the path and the guard, so the two cannot drift apart.

200.description: The account, as it is now signed in.

get.description:
No credential is required, and none is expected. This is the one endpoint on the API a caller can reach without signing in.

`data` is always an array. A catalogue with nothing in it is a `200` with `{"data": []}` - not a 404, and not `null` - so a client renders a list in both cases and never has to treat "no products" as a failure. There is no pagination envelope: `data` is the only key in the response.

`price` is a JSON number and not a string. It is stored as a fixed-scale decimal of two places and is rendered here as a bare number: no currency symbol, no thousands separator, and no guarantee of a trailing zero. A price of `5.00` is returned as `5` and a price of `124.50` as `124.5`. Both are the same JSON number and the same JavaScript value - JSON has no distinction between `5` and `5.0` - so format the value to two places for display rather than counting the places in the payload.

Field names are exactly `id`, `name` and `price`.

200.description: The catalogue. An empty catalogue is also a 200, with an empty `data` array.

get.summary: The mocked diagnosis for a described problem.
get.description:
**Mocked.** Every value below is a literal in `DiagnosisController`. Nothing is derived from a description and no request can reach the controller with one — it takes no input at all — so no model, estimator or image classifier runs behind it. The endpoint exists so the diagnosis screen has a typed shape to render while the estimator is being built, and it will answer the same thing forever.

`price_estimate` is a rupee range as integers. No symbol is carried in the payload: format at the point of display.

200.description: The mocked diagnosis.

get.summary: The mocked categories a diagnosis can be one of.
get.description:
**Mocked.** A fixed list of three, and `recommended` names one of them. It is not computed from anything and there is no ranking behind it, so the value is a choice made in the controller rather than a result.

`confidence` is a number between 0 and 1 and is not a probability of anything: nothing was scored.

200.description: The mocked suggestions.

get.summary: The mocked live position of a technician travelling to a booking.
get.description:
**Mocked.** This is the most misleading endpoint on the API, which is the reason to read its description. `location`, `distance_km` and `eta_minutes` describe a journey that is not happening: the coordinates are two fixed points, the distance and the ETA are literals, and nothing polls this endpoint or moves anything between calls. A screen that draws a map from these numbers shows a technician standing still in one place forever.

`status` is a single string and `stages` repeats each stage with its own `completed` flag, so a client never has to derive one from the other and the two cannot disagree inside a payload.

200.description: The mocked tracking state.

get.summary: The mocked list of a customer's bookings.
get.description:
**Mocked.** Two fixed bookings, with timestamps relative to the moment of the request. Nothing in the list belongs to the account whose token presented it, which is the important half: every customer receives an identical list, so a screen that renders it will look correct to whoever wrote it and be wrong to everybody.

`bookings` is always an array and there is no pagination envelope, so a caller renders a list in both the populated and the empty case and never has to treat "no bookings" as a failure.

200.description: The mocked bookings.

get.description:
**Both mocked.** Service categories with a "from" price, and two featured technicians drawn from the same roster the matching endpoint offers, so the same person appears on both screens with the same rating and the same base fee.

`price_from` is an integer in `currency` and nothing computed it — there is no pricing table in this repository. **A screen must not present it as an offer.**

There is no `tone` field. The design tints its three cards differently, and that is a colour rather than a fact about a service; the screen keys the tint off the category's own identifier instead, and falls back to a neutral card for anything it has not seen.

200.description: The mocked payload.

get.description:
**Mocked, and it ignores every sort it offers.** `filters` arrives with identifiers and labels and no behaviour: nothing reads it, and nothing reorders `technicians`. The order is the order the fixture was written, which is why the highest-rated technician is listed last — a payload that had been sorted by anything would not look like that.

`found_count` is 24 and `technicians` holds three. That is what the design draws and what a real endpoint would never do, so **a caller must not use `found_count` to decide how many cards to draw.**

`summary` describes a matching run that has not happened. It is the most persuasive string on this endpoint and the least substantiated; it is kept because the design contains it, and the front end's honesty record names it.

This endpoint takes no query parameter and ignores one if given. There is no index of technicians, no distance to compute from, no prices to compare and no reviews to rank.

200.description: The mocked payload.

get.description:
**Mocked, and this is the endpoint most likely to be mistaken for a real one.** The three estimate lines add up to `total` and nothing computed either; no technician would arrive expecting to be paid that amount. `payment_methods` is three ways to pay that no gateway in this repository can take.

**The only mocked customer endpoint that can say no.** An identifier other than `BK-2041` is refused with a `404` rather than answered with the example booking's technician — answering is exactly what an endpoint that forgot to look anything up looks like, and the screen would render it without complaint.

`dates` are `now()` plus zero, one and two, with the weekday and the day label derived from those dates rather than typed beside them. The design says "TODAY / 14 Oct", which cannot both be true; arithmetic resolves the contradiction instead of prose. `is_today` is a flag and the screen renders the word from it, because a stored "TODAY" would be asserting that a day captured in the past is still today — and these front ends are static exports served unchanged from whenever they were built.

Every `times` entry is today's, because nothing is selected: the day and the slot are both local state on a screen whose only button books nothing.

parameters.name: booking
parameters.description: The booking's identifier. Deliberately unconstrained: it is compared against one string, so any pattern that let a value through would reach the same `404`, and any pattern that turned one away would only move the failure to a route that says less about it.

200.description: The mocked payload.

post.description:
**Mocked, and it creates no account.** There is no registration in this platform: accounts exist because an operator ran `fixmate:create-account`, and that command is the only way one is made. This route echoes the `name` and `email` it was given and returns a `token` that is a random string nothing accepts. The password is accepted and ignored — not echoed, not hashed, not recorded.

**It is unreachable before an account exists.** The route sits behind `auth:sanctum` and the customer door, so presenting no token gets a `401` and presenting a worker's token gets a `403`. That is deliberate rather than an oversight: a registration form you can only reach once signed in is visibly unfinished, and the alternative is a door that looks real and stores nothing.

A `201` is returned deliberately, to match the shape the screen is written against. When registration is really built this becomes a real account creation and the `201` starts meaning something; until then it means "the screen's happy path rendered", and this description is where that is said.

201.description: A mocked success. No account was created and the token is not a credential.

bearerAuth.description: A Sanctum personal access token, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Opaque and not a JWT: read the claims it was issued with, from the `abilities` a `me` response echoes back, rather than decoding anything.

Acknowledgement.description: One message, and nothing else. Both halves of a password reset answer this way.

ValidationFailure.description:
The request was refused.

On a sign-in door this is also the answer for an unknown address, a wrong password and an account that cannot be used — all three are refused identically, under `errors.credentials`, and nothing in the response tells them apart.

refusedCredentials.summary: Credentials that do not resolve, in a store where they cannot.

value.message: These credentials do not match our records.

credentials: These credentials do not match our records.

refusedLink.summary: A reset link that is spent or has expired.

password_reset: This password reset link is no longer valid. Request a new one.

refusedPassword.summary: A new password that does not meet the policy. The link is still usable.

password: The password field must be at least 12 characters.

Unauthenticated.description: No usable token was presented. Carries a message and nothing else — in particular no stack trace, which a debug-mode exception would otherwise have appended to every refusal on this API.

Forbidden.description:
The token is valid and the caller still may not do this.

Three different situations answer here, and the message is what tells them apart: a token for another account type (which names both types, because the caller has proved they hold a working token), a token without the ability the route requires (which does not name the missing ability, because an oracle that hands out the access model one refusal at a time is the same mistake as confirming which addresses exist in a credential store), and a suspended account (which is not a signed-out state, so a front end must not send the person back to the sign-in screen).

NotFound.description: The record does not exist — answered only to a caller that was permitted to ask, so a 404 here is never a way of learning that a record exists and is merely hidden from you.

Throttled.description:
Too many attempts. Each door has its own allowance, so exhausting one does not lock the same address out of the other three.

`retry_after` is in seconds and matches the `Retry-After` header. This is the only refusal on the API that carries a second field: it is the one case where telling the caller when to come back is the useful answer.

Retry-After.description: Seconds to wait, matching `retry_after` in the body.

Conflict.description:
The caller is permitted to do this, and the request conflicts with something else. Three situations answer here and they are deliberately not 403s, because a 403 would be a false statement about why the caller was stopped: they hold the ability and passed every guard.

* Promoting or suspending the account you are signed in with. Promotion creates a *second* record, so self-promotion would leave one person holding two super administrator accounts with two token sets — and a suspension could not close both.
* Promoting somebody whose address already has a super administrator account. The unique index would refuse the insert anyway; left as a 500 it would tell the person driving the interface that the platform is broken rather than that the account is in an unusual state.

SignInAccount.description: An account as the sign-in doors return it: no status, because an account that cannot be used never gets here. There is no field for a password hash, and one could not be added without a field appearing here first.

must_change_password.description: Whether this account must replace its password before it can be used. Reported at sign-in so a front end can route to the change screen rather than to a dashboard that will refuse every request. **Advisory, not a control** — `EnsurePasswordChanged` is the control, and a client that ignores this field still cannot reach a single other endpoint.

ForgotPasswordRequest.description: An address and nothing else. The account type is not a field and must never become one.

token.description: The token from the reset link. Single use, and checked before the password, so a password refused under `errors.password` leaves the link usable.

password.description: The new password. Refused under `errors.password` when it does not meet the back end's policy.

Abilities.description: The token's own claim list, echoed back. Read it to decide what to offer before calling anything — but the back end re-checks it on every request, so hiding a button is a convenience and not the protection. `*` is the wildcard carried by a super administrator's token; `accounts:read`, `accounts:suspend` and `accounts:promote` are the named ones.

CurrentAccountResponse.description: The signed-in account, as the application that asked sees it. One shape for all four doors, unlike the sign-in responses above which nest the account under a per-type key. At sign-in each application already knows what it is; "who am I" is asked by a caller that may be holding the wrong token, so the answer has to be able to say that the thing answering is a customer when a worker was expected.

account_type.description: Which store the account is in. Read this before anything else: it is what tells a front end it is holding somebody else's token.

type.description: The account type, as the same value the sign-in path and the token abilities use. Present on every row so the directory is self-describing: it mixes four account types and a row is otherwise uninterpretable. Identifiers are only meaningful together with this — an id from one table says nothing about another.

AdminAccountResponse.description: One administrator, as the account-management surface describes it. The same four fields as the account summary, deliberately, but a separate schema: this one is what a super administrator sees when looking at *someone else*, and each account type is meant to see a different representation of the same person. Sharing one schema would make that a matter of who remembered to unset a field.

ErrorResponse.description:
The shape of every refusal on this API. There is no envelope around it and no error code, deliberately: one shape for a validation failure, an unauthenticated request, a refused request and a missing record means a client has exactly one thing to read, and a second shape would be a second thing to get right.

`additionalProperties` is false because it is load-bearing. A debug-mode exception would otherwise append the file, the line and a stack trace to one of these, and the check that the key set is exactly `message` plus `errors` is what keeps it out.

errors.description: Per-field messages, present on a 422 and absent otherwise. The keys are `credentials` on a sign-in refusal, `password_reset` for a spent or expired link, and the field's own name otherwise — the same keys the back end's feature tests assert.

ThrottledResponse.description: The only refusal on the API that carries a second field, because this is the one case where when to come back is the useful answer.

data.description: A new pair of credentials. The renewal token that was presented is spent by this call, so the one returned here replaces it and the old one must be discarded.

access_token.description: Short-lived. Held in memory and never written to browser storage.

renewal_token.description: Longer-lived, and held in browser storage. It can only mint an access token, and only once.

access_token_expires_at.description: When the access token stops being accepted.

renewal_token_expires_at.description: A hard ceiling, whether or not the token is used. Renewal rotates it; this is what stops an unused one being kept indefinitely.

must_change_password.description: Whether this account must replace its password. Reported here for the same reason it is reported at sign-in, and renewal is the only call that happens on a page reload: a front end restoring a session from browser storage has run no sign-in, so without this field the only evidence that the account is flagged would be the 403 every other route returns. Acting on that would mean matching on the back end's wording, which is a second place where that sentence's meaning is decided. The renewal itself succeeds, and the access token it returns is still refused by the guard on every route except the change and sign-out — the rule is enforced on the token's use, not on its existence.

data.description: Every account of every type, grouped by account type.

warning.description: Present and null when the super administrator role is still narrow. A sentence when it is not, describing the role as it is now rather than as it will be — a fact the reader can check rather than a prediction they have to trust.

current_password.description: The password this account is currently using. Verified against the stored hash, not against a rule: there is exactly one right answer to whether it is correct, and a wrong one is a 422 carrying the message.

password.description: The new password. Must satisfy the same policy as the reset flow, and must not be the current password — otherwise "you must change your password" could be satisfied by submitting the shared one again, and the flag cleared with nothing changed.

data.description: Every product, ordered by identifier. An empty catalogue is an empty array, never a null and never an absent key.

id.description: The product identifier. A JSON integer, and stable for the life of the product.

name.description: The product name. Never empty: an unnamed product is not a state this API can return.

price.description:
The price as a bare JSON number. **A number, not a string** - it is rendered here as `19.99` and not `"19.99"`, because the front end formats this value directly and will not coerce a string first.

The stored value is a decimal(10,2), so it always has two decimal places internally, but JSON does not carry that: a price of `5.00` is returned as `5` and `124.50` as `124.5`. These are the same JSON number and the same JavaScript value. Format to two places for display; do not read the number of places off the payload.

Money.description: A rupee range. Integers, no symbol and no decimal, because nothing here is computed and a pre-formatted string in a payload cannot be formatted again.

recommended.description: The `id` of one of the suggestions. Named rather than implied by position, so a client cannot read the wrong entry once the list is reordered.

service.description: What the technician is travelling to fix. Present because a tracker that cannot say what the job is cannot be read by the person waiting for it — "On the way" with no job attached is a progress bar.

items.description: A stage that has not happened carries a null `timestamp` rather than an absent field, so a client reading the array never has to tell "not yet" from "this payload is malformed".

status_label.description: The word the row prints, sent because `in_progress` is a database value and stripping the underscore is still a machine's idea of a phrase. `status` stays, so a caller can branch on it.

scheduled_on.description: The locale-formatted date the row prints, beside the ISO string. Four front ends should not each invent a date format — the same reasoning that put `day_label` on the quote's three dates.

has_quote.description:
Whether `GET /users/bookings/{booking}/quote` answers for this booking. **Required rather than optional**, because a screen cannot tell "this booking has no quote" from "this payload predates the field" — and defaulting it to `false` would render the second as the first, a row that cannot be opened for no reason a reader could see.

True for the booking in progress and false for the completed one, and that is not an omission: a quote is what somebody is quoted *before* agreeing to a price, and a finished job has a receipt instead — which this repository has no endpoint for.

RegistrationRequest.description: Echoed back rather than validated or stored. `password` is accepted and then ignored: it is not echoed in the response, not hashed and not recorded, so a credential never travels somewhere it does not need to be — a proxy log, a browser cache, or a screen that only wanted a name.

user.description: The two fields the design's success state shows. No phone number, because the registration frame has no phone field to echo one from.

token.description: A random string, and **not a credential**. Nothing accepts it, `auth:sanctum` cannot resolve it, and it is not recorded anywhere.

items.description: A kind of work, and the lowest price anybody might charge for it. Nothing computed that price.

A technician the carousel draws. `completed_jobs` is a volume claim rather than a rating count, even though the fixture happens to carry the same number for both — naming them the same field would have let a later fixture say somebody has done 240 jobs and been rated by 12 people with nothing looking wrong.

found_count.description: How many matches exist in total. **Not the length of `technicians`**, so it cannot be used to decide how many cards to draw.

summary.description: The sentence describing a matching run that has not happened. Kept from the design and unsubstantiated; the front end's honesty record names it.

items.description: A sort the design offers and this endpoint does not perform. Sent rather than left in the screen so its inertness is visible in one place: a server is offering to sort these results, and the list arrives in the order the fixture was written.

trade.description: The trade on its own, so four front ends each join it to `years_experience` their own way rather than receiving a bullet character in a payload.

available_now.description: Whether the card's action offers to book. Both are sent because both are needed: a screen given only the flag would have to invent "Available Now", and one given only the label would have to compare English strings to decide whether somebody can be booked.

best_match.description: The badge the design draws. **Nothing here ranked anything**; this marks a position in an array the fixture put there on purpose.

category.description: The kind of work the booking falls under. The bookings list names a category and this names the specific job, and having both is what lets the two endpoints agree about one booking.

technician.description: Deliberately **not** the tracking worker's shape. That one carries `phone` and `photo_url` as nullable because the tracker may have to show a call button; this card draws none, so the two fields are absent rather than null — a null would say "this endpoint has no value", which is not the same as "there is no value".

items.description: A day the technician could come. Computed from `now()` rather than typed in, so the three offered days are always three consecutive days.

is_today.description: A flag the screen renders the word "TODAY" from, rather than a stored "TODAY" that would be asserting a day captured in the past is still today.

label.description: The twelve-hour label the card prints, sent because that casing is a rendering decision four front ends should each make for themselves. Every slot is today's, because nothing is selected.

estimate.description: **Nothing computed any of it.** There is no pricing table, no rate card, no labour rate and no platform fee in this repository, so these three lines are the shape of a quote rather than a quote.

items.description: Amounts as integers, never as rendered strings: four front ends draw prices, and a pre-formatted string in a payload cannot be formatted again.

total.description: **Stated rather than left to be summed.** A caller that added the lines and disagreed with a total it was also sent would have no way to know which of the two was wrong.

items.description: A way of paying that this repository cannot take. There is no gateway, no checkout, no order and no payment intent anywhere.
